qs.q: A port wine stain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve is found in a child with seizures, intellectual disability, and skull "tram-track" calcifications. What underlying mutation causes this syndrome?
o: Germline VHL mutation causing haemangioblastomas and arteriovenous malformations
TSC1/TSC2 mutation causing tuberous sclerosis complex with characteristic cortical tubers
Somatic GNAQ missense mutation in the Gα subunit causing constitutive intracellular signalling
NF1 mutation causing multiple neurofibromas and characteristic café-au-lait macules
qs.e: Sturge-Weber syndrome (port wine stain + leptomeningeal angiomas + seizures + intellectual disability) is caused by a somatic GNAQ missense mutation occurring early in development — not inherited.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Intellectual disability (ID) is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by significantly reduced intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior, beginning before adulthood. Diagnosis requires standardized testing and assessment of daily living skills.

sections.p: ID is defined by an IQ < 70 plus deficits in adaptive functioning that appear during the developmental period. Diagnosis uses age‑appropriate IQ tests and adaptive behavior scales (e.g., Vineland).
b: IQ < 70 on standardized test
Significant limitation in communication, self‑care, home, school, or community skills
Onset before 18 years

sections.p: Severity is graded by IQ and adaptive level, guiding support needs.
b: Mild: IQ 50‑69, can achieve academic skills with support
Moderate: IQ 35‑49, needs supervised living and vocational training
Severe: IQ 20‑34, requires extensive daily assistance
Profound: IQ < 20, total dependence for all activities

sections.p: Causes are grouped into genetic, prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal factors; genetics account for the majority of cases worldwide.
b: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) – most common chromosomal cause
Fragile X syndrome – leading monogenic cause, especially in males
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder – common in low‑resource settings
Congenital infections (TORCH: CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis, HIV) – prevalent where prenatal care is limited
Perinatal hypoxia‑ischemia – birth asphyxia in low‑resource hospitals
Nutritional deficiencies (iodine, severe protein‑energy malnutrition)
Sickle cell disease complications (stroke) in endemic regions

sections.p: Children show delayed milestones, limited speech, poor problem‑solving, and difficulty with self‑care. Behavioral issues such as hyperactivity or autistic traits may coexist.
b: Failure to achieve age‑appropriate language and motor milestones
Limited eye contact, poor joint attention
Difficulty following simple instructions
Frequent tantrums or self‑injurious behavior

sections.p: Testing aims to identify a reversible or treatable cause and to classify the etiology.

t.b: Detects large chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., trisomy 21, microdeletions) – a positive result confirms a genetic etiology
Identifies CGG repeat expansion – a positive result explains X‑linked ID

t.a: Serology for TORCH infections (CMV IgM, rubella IgM, HIV ELISA)
t.b: Detects congenital infections – guides antiviral or antiretroviral therapy
Shows structural anomalies (e.g., cortical malformations) – informs prognosis and surgical options
Screens for hypothyroidism, a reversible cause of developmental delay

sections.p: Certain features suggest urgent medical issues or worsening prognosis.
b: Severe feeding difficulties leading to aspiration pneumonia
Unexplained seizures or regression of skills
Rapid weight loss or failure to thrive despite adequate nutrition
Signs of treatable metabolic disease (e.g., ketoacidosis)

sections.p: Management combines cause‑specific therapy, early intervention, and lifelong support.
b: Treat underlying cause: antiretroviral therapy for HIV, thyroid hormone replacement, seizure control with antiepileptics
Early childhood intervention: speech, occupational, and physiotherapy
Behavioral programs (ABA) for autism‑like features
Educational accommodations and vocational training for mild/moderate ID
Family counseling and respite care

sections.p: Regular monitoring of growth, development, and comorbidities is essential.
b: Annual developmental assessment and adaptive‑skill review
Screen for vision, hearing, and dental problems
Vaccination updates, especially for pneumococcal and influenza
Genetic counseling for families planning future pregnancies

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic or overlap with ID.
b: Autism spectrum disorder – may have normal IQ but severe social communication deficits
Global developmental delay – used for children <5 years before IQ can be measured
Learning disability – specific academic deficits with average intelligence
Normal karyotype does not exclude microdeletions – consider microarray
Mildly elevated thyroid antibodies may be incidental – correlate with TSH/T4
IQ testing in severe sensory impairment can underestimate true ability

whenToSeekHelp: Acute loss of previously acquired skills
Severe feeding difficulty with choking or aspiration

faq.a: Most causes are permanent, but treatable conditions (e.g., hypothyroidism, infections) can improve function if identified early.
Severity is based on IQ ranges and adaptive‑behavior scores, guiding the level of support needed.
It identifies specific syndromes, informs prognosis, and provides recurrence risk information for families.

exam: List the three diagnostic criteria for intellectual disability.
Describe the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability and its key clinical features.
Explain the work‑up steps to identify a reversible cause in a child with newly diagnosed intellectual disability.
